items.title: The Art of Dignity Beyond Pride: How to Move Through Heartbreak Like Frida Kahlo
items.description: “Life will break you,” Louise Erdrich wrote in her exquisite insistence that “you are here to risk your heart.” The price we pay for the risk is the great equalizer of humanity. items.title: How to Get Love Less Wrong: George Saunders on Breaking the Patterns that Break Our Hearts
items.description: "We want to believe that love is singular and exclusive, and it unnerves us to think that it might actually be renewable..."

items.title: How to Help Someone Change: The Samurai Guide to Giving Feedback
items.description: Few things in life are more exasperating than seeing the potential in someone you love and seeing them continually fall short of it, stumbling again and again over the same self-erected roadblocks of character and conduct, comporting themselves in a manner painfully inferior to what you know them to be capable of. items.title: How to Grow Old: Bertrand Russell on What Makes a Fulfilling Life
items.description: "Make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal, until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede, and your life becomes increasingly merged in the universal life."

items.title: The Wild Iris: Nobel Laureate Louise Glück on the Door at the End of Your Suffering
items.description: "Whatever returns from oblivion returns to find a voice."

items.title: How to Bear Your Sorrows: Nick Cave on Integrating the Darkness of Loss with the Bright Ongoingness of Life
items.description: Few things in our culture are more wounding than the concept of healing — as if the pains and losses that we suffer are an illness, a malfunction of the psyche to be cut out like a tumor, rather than a natural function of being alive, of feeling life deeply and living it fully. items.title: How to Spot and How to Stop a Liar: Hannah Arendt on Deception, Self-Deception, and the Psychology of Defactualization
items.description: "No matter how large the tissue of falsehood that an experienced liar has to offer, it will never be large enough ... to cover the immensity of factuality."

items.title: Do Not Spare Yourself
items.description: The only thing more dangerous than wanting to save another person — a dangerous desire too often mistaken for love — is wanting to save yourself, to spare yourself the disappointment and heartbreak and loss inseparable from being a creature with hopes and longings constantly colliding with reality, with the indifference of time and chance, with the opposing hopes and longings of others. items.title: Marcus Aurelius on the Good Luck of Your Bad Luck: The Stoic Strategy for Weathering Life’s Waves and Turning Suffering into Strength
items.description: "What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on."

items.title: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love
items.description: "When you love someone, the best thing you can offer that person is your presence."

items.title: Pythagoras on the Purpose of Life and the Meaning of Wisdom
items.description: Abiding insight into the aim of human existence from the man who revolutionized science and coined the word "philosopher."

items.title: Fernando Pessoa on Unselfing into Who You Really Are
items.description: “To be nobody-but-yourself — in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else — means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight,” E. E. Cummings wrote in his timeless summons for the courage to be yourself. items.title: Is There a God? Stephen Hawking Gives the Definitive Answer to the Eternal Question
items.description: "The universe is the ultimate free lunch."

items.title: Diseases of the Will: Neuroscience Founding Father Santiago Ramón y Cajal on the Six Psychological Flaws That Keep the Gifted from Living Up to Their Gift
items.description: "Our neurons must be used ... not only to know but also to transform knowledge; not only to experience but also to construct."

items.title: Nick Cave on the Antidote to Our Existential Helplessness
items.description: Stepping up to the subtle gestures that can redeem a day, or a life.
